result.summary: A run of short fragments from Hesiod's Catalogues of Women, quoted by ancient writers. They cover the Arcadian city Pallantium, the golden ram of Phrixus and Helle, the blinding of Phineus, and the Sons of Boreas chasing the Harpies past the strange peoples at the edge of the world.

scenes.title: Scattered fragments on Arcadia and Phineus
scenes.summary: Short quotations and notes name Pallantium, Meliboea and Phellus, and the ram of Phrixus. They also give two reasons for the blinding of Phineus, and the Harpies carrying him to the milk-feeders.

scenes.title: Sons of Boreas pursue the Harpies
scenes.summary: A papyrus fragment follows the Sons of Boreas as they chase the Harpies past the Massagetae, Pygmies, Libyans, Hyperboreans, Etna, Ortygia and the Cephallenians.
scenes.stakes: The Harpies are trying to escape capture by the pursuing Sons of Boreas.

scenes.title: Fates of the Harpies; strange peoples
scenes.summary: Later writers report where the Harpies fled and where the pursuers turned back and prayed. Others defend Hesiod's accounts of the Pygmies and similar peoples.

notable_quotes.reason: Strabo defends Hesiod's knowledge of far peoples such as the Pygmies.

analysis.text: The fragments show Hesiodic poetry mixing genealogy with geography, linking heroes and peoples to gods and the edges of the known world.
These are only quotations preserved by scholars, so Hesiod's original context is lost, and ancient critics already argued over his strange peoples.

legacy.text: The golden ram and the Harpy chase became standard parts of the Argonaut story, notably in Apollonius Rhodius's Argonautica.

fun_facts.text: The longest piece here survives on a third-century A.D. papyrus from Oxyrhynchus in Egypt.

language_notes.text: 'Bare' is an archaic past tense of 'bear'; the line says Meliboea gave birth to Phellus.
The torch's context is lost; the fragment survives only as an example of a peculiar word form quoted by a grammarian.
Phineus revealed to Phrixus the road to Colchis, and was punished by the gods; the alternative story says he chose long life over sight.
'Milk-feeders' (Galactophagi) are nomadic peoples of the northern steppe, who live on milk and travel in wagons.
The Massagetae, Half-Dog men, Underground-folk and Pygmies are real or legendary peoples at the edges of the known world, as Greeks imagined it.
"Whose thought passes their utterance" means people whose words outrun their understanding, who speak rashly and so fall under the gods' power.
The Hyperboreans were a legendary people living far north, beyond Boreas the North Wind. Eridanus is a legendary river linked with amber.
Calypso detained Odysseus on her island, as told in the Odyssey. Poseidon's anger at Odysseus is the reason given here.
The name Harpys is explained as coming from the Harpy who fell there. Such origin stories for place names are common in Greek myth.
Strophades comes from the Greek for "turning", which fits the story that the pursuers turned back there.
Troglodytes means "cave-dwellers", a name for peoples thought to live in caves, usually in Ethiopia and the Red Sea region.

context_notes.text: These 'fragments' are ancient quotations by later writers, since the Catalogues of Women survive only in pieces.
Iphiclus was a hero sometimes listed among the Argonauts, the crew who sailed with Jason for the Golden Fleece.
Nephele, a cloud nymph, sent the golden ram to rescue her children Phrixus and Helle from their stepmother's plot.
The Harpies were winged female spirits who snatched things away and tormented Phineus; here they instead carry him to a distant land.
Epaphus was son of Zeus and Io, and ancestor of the peoples of Libya and Aethiopia in Greek tradition.
The Sons of Boreas, Zetes and Calais, were winged heroes who drove the Harpies from Phineus in the Argonaut story.
A scholiast is an ancient commentator whose notes preserve quotations and variants from lost works like this one.
Strabo, a Greek geographer, defends Hesiod against charges of ignorance about distant peoples.

literary_notes.text: 'Famous' and 'good spear-man' are formulaic epic descriptors, typical of catalogue poetry that praises ancestors.
'Resounding thud' imitates the noise of many feet, making the crowd or dance audible.
The list of far-off peoples is typical of the poem's catalogue style, giving the chase a vast geographic scale.
Phrases like "mare-milking Scythians" and "lord of oracles" use fixed descriptive epithets in the epic manner.
"Fruitless air" echoes the barren sea, giving a bleak picture of the Harpies' endless flight.
